To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a policy of recommending PrEP to high-risk MSM/TGW (those reporting condomless receptive intercourse) would yield an estimated 1-year reduction in HIV incidence of 1.95%, and would require PrEP to be rolled out to 59.7%.

a policy recommending PrEP only for men who have sex exclusively with men and transgender women (MSM/TGW) reporting condomless receptive sex in the last three months is identical to the policy that prioritizes those MSM/TGW with the highest expected benefit from PrEP, and that this policy is nearly identical to the policy recommended by the US Centers of Disease Control (CDC).
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing guidelines to inform the rollout of PrE
identifying subpopulations of at-risk MSM/TGW for whom PrEP is most likely to have the highest benefit.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the approach we took could potentially be employed to develop a PrEP policy for other at-risk population and resource-limited setting.

the policy that prioritizes PrEP for high risk subpopulations of MSMTGW, as identified by the statistical models, is identical to the policy that prioritises PrEP for high expected PrEP beneficiaries, and is similar in impact to the CDC PrEP guideline, which recommends PrEP to a wider range of MSMTGW.

a policy recommending PrEP for a subpopulation of MSM reporting condomless receptive sex in the last 3 month is identical to that of a policy prioritizing MSM with the highest PrEP benefit, and would achieve a similar reduction in HIV incidence at the same level of PrEP coverage as that recommended by the US CDC.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the population impact of PrEP policies can be estimated by using a small set of behavioral risk factors, and that such policies are likely to be more efficient than those which recommend PrEP to the entire target population.

a policy recommending PrEP based on high risk of HIV infection without PrEP is identical to that recommending PrEP based solely on high expected PrEP benefits, and both policies are nearly identical to the policy recommended by the US Centers of Disease Control.

a PrEP policy that recommends PrEP to high-risk subpopulates of MSM/TGW based on demographic and behavioural characteristics can achieve similar population impact as a PrEP policy based on a larger number of behavioural risk factors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
policies recommending PrEP based on behavioral risk factors can be effective at reducing HIV incidence in resource-limited populations.
PrEP can be effectively targeted to a subpopulation of MSM, and that the PrEP guidelines currently being developed for MSM should consider this approach to optimize PrEP benefit and minimize costs.

PrEP can be effective for reducing HIV incidence among high-risk subpopu- lations of MSM/TGW, and that PrEP can have a population impact that rivals that of other prevention interventions, such as male circumcision, if PrEP is prioritized to the highest risk subpopulations of at-risk populations.
